statements.quote: In a pre-registered lab experiment, we assigned 302 university students tasks involving the creation of ideas for generating creative pictures, with a randomly selected subset granted access to ChatGPT.

We conducted a pre-registered laboratory experiment, in which we recruited 302 students to complete four novel creative tasks, with a random subsample of participants having access to generative AI technologies.
The choice of evaluation method evolved as our experiment progressed, and we explain the process and the rationale for our final choice in the Supplementary Materials (Sections 1.2 and 1.3).

After the first wave of the experiment, we followed the prevailing approach in the literature by using average ratings from two evaluators as a measure of the creative performance, as reported in our earlier working paper (Zhu and Zou, 2023). The current analysis differs in two respects: (1) each of the two main tasks was evaluated by a new panel of thirty independent raters after the introduction of a training treatment in the second experimental wave, and (2) the evaluations now incorporate both textual and visual components of the submitted ideas. We are grateful to a previous editor for encouraging these refinements.
For examples of participants’ submitted ideas and the corresponding final images, please see Section 3.5 of the Supplementary Materials.

Our experimental design and intended analyses were pre-registered at AsPredicted.org. We provide the pre-registration and discuss our deviations in Section 1 of the Supplementary Material.

Section 3 of the Supplementary Materials provides the instructions used in the formal experimental sessions, the training materials for the training sessions, the instructions for evaluators, and screenshots of the experimental interface.

We provide results from a battery of robustness analyses in the Supplementary Materials. We find that the results reported above are robust to using standardized grades instead of the non-standardized grades as the dependent variable (Table S1), separating the second and third tasks by theme (Tables S2 and S3), altering the data structure by analyzing the data either at the individual/team level (Table S4) or at the idea-evaluator level (Table S5). The results are also robust if we exclude a random set of 10 evaluators (out of the 30) for each task (see Table S6), or only include the two evaluators whose grades yield the highest alpha values (Table S7).

The inverted U-shaped pattern also emerges when we divide the sample into quartiles based on the DAT score and separately estimate the treatment effects for these four subsamples (see Figure S1 in the Supplementary Material).

These variables only exhibit limited explanatory power of the treatment effects, and the correlation between the performance and the self-reported contribution seems to be opposite for the image-text grades and the text-only grades (see the columns 2–5 of Tables S9 and S10 in the Supplementary Material, as well as columns 3 and 7 of Table 7).
Data will be made available on request.

Author contributions: While both authors were involved in most stages in this project, W.Z. took a leading role in conceptualization, experimental design, making analysis plan and writing the article, and F.Z. took a leading role in programming the experimental interface, managing the experimental procedure and data curation, and conducting and presenting the formal analysis.

We utilized the machine translation API from Alibaba cloud to translate all Chinese words into English, which were then used to calculate the DAT score based on GloVe algorithm (Pennington et al., 2014) using the pre-trained word vectors from common crawl (840B tokens, 2.2 million vocabulary, 300-dimension vectors).
The address for Alibaba cloud is: https://www.alibabacloud.com/product/machine-translation.

We used the OpenAI API to extract five keywords (restricted to nouns) from each submitted output. Specifically, we employed the GPT-4.1 model, which OpenAI described as its “smartest non-reasoning model” as of September 2025.

We first conducted text segmentation for both submission texts and ChatGPT answer texts, using Python module Jieba. After that, we removed special characters such as punctuation marks, and escape characters. Then we calculated ratio of words in final submissions that is also in the ChatGPT answers, which we defined as Overlap Percentage.
Supplementary material related to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2026.107414.

deposits.notes: This entry records the supplementary-material location explicitly cited in Appendix E (p. 21); it is not a confirmed participant-data deposit. The DOI request returned HTTP 200 at https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0167268126000028, but that page is only a redirect wrapper. The publisher landing page https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167268126000028 returned HTTP 403, so its supplementary file list and contents could not be checked. No access barrier was bypassed and no file URL was guessed. The paper describes the supplement as containing the preregistration/deviations, instructions, training/evaluation materials, examples of ideas/images, and additional analyses (pp. 2, 6, 8, 10, 13). That description does not establish a complete participant-level dataset or participant-linked texts. File count, sizes, contents, study coverage, and license remain unconfirmed.

notes: Checked on 2026-10-09. Read the complete saved journal-version markdown (22 PDF pages, including Appendices A-E and references) in chunks, and checked all 18 recorded quotations against the corresponding PDF-page text. Quotes preserve the wording; line wrapping and typographic ligatures were normalized for verification, and the quoted fragments avoid attached footnote markers. The primary evidence is the p. 15 Data availability statement: 'Data will be made available on request.' The form's data_and_code supplies no data or code URL. No study-specific data repository or public participant-level file was identified or read. The one entry in deposits is the paper's publisher supplementary-material location; it does not represent confirmed public data. AsPredicted.org is named without a registration number or study-specific URL. Its homepage returned HTTP 200; the linked lookup page https://aspredicted.org/lookup1.php also returned HTTP 200 and requires a registration number, which this PDF does not provide. No lookup was submitted. No code-release URL is stated. The OSF DOI in the references belongs to Hubert et al., not to c150, and was excluded as a deposit for this paper. The earlier SSRN version cited in the references (4676053) and the candidate-record lead (5196748) both returned HTTP 403. No repository file API could be called for this paper because no study-specific repository identifier was found. The successful DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse and OSF title/author searches and their limits are recorded above; transient Zenodo errors were resolved with permitted unauthenticated requests. Public data have not been confirmed for calculating per-person means, SDs or SEs by arm, resolving Table 2 SD aggregation, reconstructing Table 5 grade distributions/CV/Gini uncertainty, fitting the exact DAT regressions and obtaining per-arm DAT counts, counting distinct people in image-text analyses, or computing diversity from participant-linked ideas. These open items remain unresolved. Confidence is medium because the explicit on-request statement is clear, but the publisher supplement was inaccessible and the broad DataCite author search was not exhaustively reviewed.
